title: The competitor digest nobody tested
scenario:
You are head of marketing operations at a mid-size software company. It is October 2026. A product marketer, Dana, built three agent prototypes over a weekend, without code, for a weekly competitor-news digest. She wants to roll one out to all 300 staff next Monday.

You must approve or change the plan. The exhibit shows Dana's notes.
exhibit:
Competitor digest: rollout notes (made-up example data)

Prototype 1: OpenAI Agent Builder workflow (visual canvas)
  Status: works in preview

Prototype 2: Claude Code Desktop scheduled task on Dana's laptop
  Schedule: Mondays 8:00
  Note: laptop is usually closed until 10:00 on Mondays

Prototype 3: Google AI Studio agents playground, "research" template
  Prompt: "Find everything about our competitors."
  Note: first test ran 40 minutes; cost not checked

Rollout plan
  - share with all 300 staff on day 1
  - tests so far: none ("the output looks good")
  - owner after launch: not named

questions.prompt: What is the biggest problem with building the digest on prototype 1?

options.text: Visual canvases can't search the web, so the digest would always be empty.
options.explanation: The exhibit says it works in preview. The problem is the product's future, not its features.

options.text: Agent Builder needs a ChatGPT Edu plan, which a software company can't buy.
options.explanation: The cited docs don't say this. The real issue is the shutdown date.

options.text: OpenAI is deprecating Agent Builder; it is scheduled to shut down on 30 November 2026.
options.explanation: Right. A new rollout would need migrating within weeks, and OpenAI's guide says the export doesn't guarantee every behaviour transfers unchanged.

options.text: Nothing: a workflow that works in preview will keep working the same way for years.
options.explanation: OpenAI's docs give a shutdown date for Agent Builder. Products change fast.

questions.prompt: What will happen with prototype 2 on a normal Monday, according to Claude Code's docs?

options.text: It runs at 8:00 in the cloud, whether or not the laptop is open.
options.explanation: That describes a cloud routine. A Desktop task runs on the laptop.

options.text: It is skipped at 8:00, then one catch-up run starts when the laptop wakes.
options.explanation: Right. Local tasks run only while the app is open and the computer is awake. Desktop then starts one catch-up run for the missed time.

options.text: It runs at 8:00, because scheduled tasks wake a closed laptop by themselves, even on a Monday.
options.explanation: The docs say closing the lid still puts the computer to sleep, and tasks don't run while it sleeps.

options.text: It never runs again after one missed time, until Dana creates the task again.
options.explanation: The docs describe a catch-up run after a missed time. The task is not deleted.

questions.prompt: Prototype 3 ran 40 minutes on one prompt. What does Google's AI Studio page advise?

options.text: Set clear stop criteria and a narrow scope, for example "five competitors, last 7 days, then stop".
options.explanation: Right. The Gemini API docs say one prompt can lead to unbounded token use, and advise clear termination criteria and a narrow scope. Templates also call the Gemini API with your key.

options.text: Nothing: the playground is free, so long runs don't matter, and nobody pays for tokens at all.
options.explanation: The Gemini API docs warn that templates call the Gemini API with your key, which can add token charges.

options.text: Make the prompt broader, so the agent finds everything in one run and stops much sooner than before.
options.explanation: A broader prompt gives the agent more to do. The Gemini API docs advise a narrow scope.

options.text: Run it more often, so each run has less news to read and finishes more quickly than a long one.
options.explanation: Running more often doesn't stop an open-ended prompt from running long. The fix is in the prompt's scope and stop rule.

questions.prompt: What should happen before the digest is shared with 300 staff?

options.text: Share it now; staff feedback is the best test, and any issues can be fixed later in the week.
options.explanation: Then 300 people see untested output. The cookbook tests first and keeps a new agent private to its maker.

options.text: Name an owner, test it on past weeks against a human digest, then share with a small group.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's cookbook tests the agent on a past meeting against a human-written brief, and a new agent is by default available only to its maker.

options.text: Add the line "be accurate" to the instructions, then share it with everyone on the staff list.
options.explanation: An instruction is not a test. Nobody would know if the output is right.

options.text: Build all three prototypes and share all of them, so staff can choose the one they like.
options.explanation: That triples the untested output and the work to maintain, with still no owner.
